summary: This bill requires parties and their counsel in any civil action to disclose in writing to the court and other parties the identity of any third party entitled to a contingent payment based on the case outcome, and to produce related agreements for inspection, with exceptions for certain loans and attorney fees.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends Title 28 to require disclosure of third-party litigation funding agreements in civil cases. It contains no provisions related to federal spending, appropriations, or budget authority.
The bill addresses disclosure requirements for contingent payment rights in civil litigation. It has no provisions concerning tax rates, tax policy, or revenue collection.
The legislation is limited to procedural transparency rules in civil actions and does not engage with healthcare delivery, insurance, or medical policy.
No provisions in the bill relate to firearms, gun ownership, or regulation of weapons.
The bill does not address immigration status, border policy, visas, or enforcement.
The bill contains no language regarding reproductive rights or abortion access.
No provisions concern military funding, defense policy, or armed forces.
The bill is silent on environmental regulations, climate policy, or natural resource management.
No provisions relate to welfare programs, entitlements, or social assistance.
The legislation does not address schools, education funding, or school choice.
No provisions concern controlled substances, decriminalization, or drug enforcement.
The bill applies exclusively to civil actions and does not affect criminal procedure, sentencing, or policing.
The bill contains no provisions on tariffs, trade agreements, or import/export policy.
No fiscal or debt-related provisions are present.
The bill does not address legal protections or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions relate to foreign assistance or international aid.
The bill does not address voting rights, election procedures, or campaign finance.
While the bill requires disclosure of certain agreements, it is narrowly focused on litigation funding and does not regulate technology companies or data privacy standards.
No provisions concern labor rights, collective bargaining, or union activities.
The bill does not address religious exemptions or anti-discrimination protections.
